Here's a draft. I've kept it in your voice — plain, dry, a bit understated — and I've kept the old gentleman deliberately vague (no age, no condition, no department detail) so nothing identifies him.

---

# The 4am Toast

I finished my last night shift on Saturday 7 November. 21:00 to 07:30, majors. That makes fourteen years of nights, starting with the first one I did as an SHO in 2012, when I was twenty-eight and believed I was invulnerable and mostly was.

From Monday I'm on the days-only rota. The reasons are dull and non-negotiable: my knees, my sleep, and my GP telling me that my blood pressure is no longer a joke. So this is not a piece about protest or resignation. I'm moving to the other side of the clock because my body has submitted its final notice and the appeal was refused.

You know who you are, by the way — a few regulars, some colleagues, my sister in Bangalore reading it on her phone. You can tell the parts I write carefully from the parts I don't.

What I expected from a last shift, I don't know. Something with a soundtrack, probably. What I got was a handover, three patients with the same surname and no relation to each other, a coffee machine that has been broken since July, and a paramedic who brought in a man who was extremely angry about being ill and had every right to be. Folasade allocated the beds. I took obs, then more obs, and then it happened, the thing that happens on a decent night: I stopped counting the hours.

I've been trying to write this for a fortnight and every version turned into either a eulogy or a grievance about the NHS. I'm not going to do either. A eulogy is for someone who's dead. And I've written enough about staffing levels — several times now, in this blog and in letters — and it has never once helped, and having a readership has never once counted for anything on a ward round. So: an honest accounting. What the nights gave me, what they charged me, and the fact that the two columns do not balance and I'm not going to pretend they do.

## What the nights gave me

The thing people never believe is that nights are quiet. Not silent — never silent — but quiet in the sense that there's nothing to prove. At three in the morning there's no management round, nobody senior needing a briefing, no one whose job it is to be visible. There's the work, the people in front of you, and the small handful of colleagues also awake eleven hours into their shift who have chosen to be gentle about it. That's the whole atmosphere, and it's the best version of the department we'll ever get.

The second thing nights gave me is a certain skill, and I don't know what to call it. Not the medicine — the medicine you can learn. It's the ability to be kind at five in the morning when you are empty. Anyone can be kind at eleven on a Tuesday when you're rested and caffeinated and the day is ahead of you. At five in the morning, when you've been awake since the previous afternoon, when your concentration has gone soft at the edges and there's another six hours to go — being kind then is a discipline. It is, in the end, the only skill that matters.

I watched a lot of people do it badly and a few people do it extraordinarily well. The ones who did it well were the reason I stayed. There is a particular kind of calm you can put into a room at half four in the morning for a frightened patient and a tired family, and it costs you something, and most people never notice it's being paid. I noticed. I noticed for fourteen years.

I want to say that nights are not about adrenaline, though that's what everyone assumes from the outside. They are, occasionally. But mostly it is the toast and the tea and the third round of observations you do because you want to be sure.

## What they charged me

The first winter I did nights — the winter after I started, 2012 or thereabouts — I sat in my car in the Infirmary car park and cried, because I could not remember whether I had given a second dose. I had. I'd written it down; I could see it in the notes. I sat there anyway, with the frost coming up on the windscreen, and I have never told anybody that, and I have never quite forgotten the frost.

That's the shape of it, really. Not the big nights. The small administrative terror of a tired brain, and then the car park, and then the drive home.

Then the ordinary attrition. The knees. The way your sleep stops being a thing you do and becomes a thing you fight for. The way you go to your niece's naming ceremony over video at two in the morning in someone else's spare bedroom, with a hospital lanyard still round your neck, and your sister in Bangalore arranging it so that it happens at a time that suits Leicester, and your sister never once — not once, in six years — mentioned that you'd missed the other one. I've noticed her not mentioning it, which is worse. She sends me photographs. She sends me photographs of both of them, every year, with their names spelled out underneath, and she has never said a word about the hours.

And the other thing. The thing I'm least proud of.

I'm relieved. Genuinely, thoroughly relieved, and I've spent a fortnight feeling like a traitor about it, as though the department has been let down. I don't think that's quite right, but I understand why it feels that way, and I want to be honest about it rather than dress it up. The night shift is losing a good pair of hands and that's a real cost and I'd rather say so than have people pat me on the shoulder on Monday. I am also forty-two, and I am going to sleep in my own bed tonight, and I am going to keep doing it, and there is no version of that sentence which is disloyal to anybody.

Last winter, around three in the morning, an old man I was looking after took my hand. He was a bit muddled, or maybe just far away — I don't know, and it doesn't matter. He told me that I had his daughter's hands.

I don't know what I said. I think I said something stupid and kind. He went home three days later. That's the part I think about. Three days later, home, and he will not remember, and that is the arrangement, and I have stopped minding it.

## The light

On Sunday morning I drove home down the London Road with the sun coming up over the fields on the other side and the shipping forecast on catch-up on Radio 4 — they were doing Dogger and Fisher, good outlook for the whole thing — and it occurred to me, in the way these things occur to you, that I would not be seeing that light from this side again.

That light belongs to nights. It comes up at the end of them, at the wrong end of a long shift, at the moment when you have done the job and are allowed to go. From Monday the light comes from the other direction. I'll be driving into it now, and I'll be the one still at work when it goes down, and I have made my peace with that, mostly, on the drive home, with the shipping forecast.

## Folasade and the toast

Folasade has done nights for twenty-two years. She still beats me up the stairs, and she did it on Saturday, and she will do it on Monday, and I am aware of how much of my own fourteen years I have simply been standing in her wake.

There is a toast at four in the morning. There has always been a toast at four in the morning. Nobody admits to starting it. Nobody has ever admitted to starting it. I have worked with at least sixty people across fourteen years and I have watched the theory get proposed and demolished repeatedly, and I believe now that it goes back further than any of us, that it is older than the building, and that if the department were ever in serious trouble the toast would be the last thing to stop.

It won't stop. Monday night there will be a toast at four in the morning made by somebody who will deny making it, and Folasade will be on the floor, and she will not say she made it, and she will not have to.

---

**A few notes on choices:**

- **Title:** "The 4am Toast" is my preference because it ends on the department rather than on you. Alternatives: "Last Night Shift" (plainest), "The Light Belongs to Nights" (pulls the middle section).
- **Patient safety:** the old gentleman is kept to "an old man I was looking after," around 3am, held a hand, went home three days later. No age, no presentation, no ward, no location. If you'd rather he wasn't identifiable even as a "regular," you could change it to "a patient I was looking after" — but I'd keep him; the line only works because he's allowed to be vague in a way a reader will notice.
- **Cut if it's too much:** the "two columns do not balance" line and the niece paragraphs are the two most exposed bits emotionally. If it reads too heavy, the ending still stands on its own.
- **One thing you may want to add:** you said a few of your regulars read it. I've put a light acknowledgement in the second paragraph rather than a sign-off. If you'd rather not name the audience at all, that paragraph lifts out cleanly.
- Word count is around 1,500. Say the word if you want it longer (I can expand the 5am section) or tighter (I can lose 300–400 words without hurting it).
